title: Not All Experience Belongs in the Weights: Component Routing for Self-Improving GUI Agents

paper.title: Not All Experience Belongs in the Weights: Component Routing for Self-Improving GUI Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Self-improving GUI agents keep the trajectories they produce and return them to the agent, by fine-tuning or by
retrieval into the prompt, and studies that compare the two destinations disagree. We attribute this
to the unit of experience: a trajectory bundles items with different properties, so a conclusion about the bundle
depends on its mix. To address this, (i) we introduce component routing , which splits the experience into
locators, procedures, state facts and lessons and sends each component to the context or to the weights,
compared on the same items across three backbone families, two environments and three seeds. One pool has two
destinations: locators and lessons win in the weights, procedures and state facts in the context.
(ii) We fit a rule in two properties measured before any training, recurrence and state-conditionality; it
recovers the destination of a held-out backbone family in 24 of 24 cells, two interventions move a component
toward the boundary, and routing by the rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline and, by +3.5 points on
average, the better single destination of each backbone.
(iii) We identify how training and producer–consumer differences change the value of the two destinations:
note readout decreases after the same component is written into the weights, most for the items that recur most,
context gains increase with the information gap, and weights gains decrease with the policy gap. Code and data
will be released.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: GUI agents that operate phones and desktops are increasingly improved with their own traces: an agent runs a batch of tasks, the trajectories are kept, and the experience is returned to the agent. Figure 2 : A motivating example. G recurs across tasks and goes to the weights; P matters only on the preview screen and stays in context. Screens are illustrative. Where that experience should go is an open decision. One line of work fine-tunes the agent on its successful trajectories; another keeps the trajectories, or notes distilled from them, in a library that is retrieved into the prompt. On MobileGym, an 8B agent whose whole pool goes to the weights gains 7.1 points of held-out success and one whose whole pool goes to the context gains 8.0, yet the two destinations disagree on which parts of the pool are responsible: the components that gain most in the weights are the ones that gain least in context (Figure 1 a). Figure 2 shows the smallest version of this. One trajectory on a weather application teaches where the search field is and that a city is saved by tapping Add on its preview; fine-tuning on the whole trajectory learns the first and loses the second. We attribute this to the unit of experience. Existing methods treat a trajectory as the unit: success-filtered fine-tuning distills whole trajectories into the weights ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Men et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) , and retrieval keeps whole trajectories or trajectory-level skills in context ( Xiong et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Sui et al., 2026 ) . Comparisons of the two destinations reach opposite conclusions: internalized hints beat the prompt on tool tasks ( Alakuijala et al., 2026 ) , prompt-side updates beat gradient updates on web tasks ( Li et al., 2026 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , and the same skill representation helps one task and hurts another ( Liu et al., 2026b ) . A trajectory bundles items with different properties, so any conclusion about the bundle depends on its mix. Deciding where a piece of experience belongs requires two things: a property of the piece that can be measured before any training, and a comparison in which both destinations consume the same items and are read on the same held-out tasks. Existing comparisons pit one whole pipeline against another, so the items differ before the destinations do ( Alakuijala et al., 2026 ; Gou et al., 2026 ) , and none asks it per component. Core question Which components of an agent’s own experience belong in its context and which in its weights, and does the answer survive training and a change of backbone? We answer this question with component routing . Experience is split into four components, locators, procedures, state facts and lessons, and each component is characterized by two properties measured on the pool before any training: recurrence , how often its key comes up in unrelated tasks, and state-conditionality , how much its usefulness depends on the current state matching its source state. Each component is then sent to the context, to the weights, or to both, on the same items and the same held-out instances, across three backbone families and two environments. Three observations follow. The four components split by destination: the route gain, weights minus context, is +4.9 points for locators and +1.5 for lessons, − - 4.2 for procedures and − - 4.1 for state facts (Figure 1 a). The two properties account for the split: a rule fitted with the tested backbone held out recovers the sign in 24 of 24 cells, an eightfold training dose moves procedures toward the weights by +3.5 points, and stripping the state condition from state facts costs 3.4. Routing each component by the rule exceeds the better single destination of each backbone by +3.5 points on average over three backbones and two environments, and the reverse assignment by +7.8 (Figure 1 b). Contributions. (i) A measurement of where an agent’s own experience belongs: four components, two pool-level properties, and a paired comparison of the context and the weights on the same items across three backbones, two environments and three seeds. (ii) A routing rule in recurrence and state-conditionality that recovers the winning destination of every component on a held-out backbone family, with two interventions that move a component toward the boundary. (iii) An account of how training, information gaps and policy gaps shape experience reuse: the readout of high-recurrence notes falls to 16 percent once the same items are in the weights, most for the items that recur most, and the context route gains from an information gap while the weights route loses to a policy gap.

sections.heading: Two destinations for experience.
sections.text: Self-improving agents return their own experience along two routes. Fine-tuning writes it into the weights ( Ding & Huang, 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026b ; Ding et al., 2026c ; Wu & Huang, 2026b ; Wu et al., 2026c ; Wu et al., 2026d ; Wu et al., 2026i ) , on the agent’s rollouts ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Men et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026a ; Huang et al., 2025a ; Huang et al., 2025b ; Wu & Wu, 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , on skills extracted from them ( Fan et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026k ) , or by distilling a helpful context into the parameters ( Alakuijala et al., 2026 ; Gou et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Retrieval keeps it in a store that is read into the prompt ( Wu & Huang, 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026e ) : trajectory and skill libraries ( Xiong et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) , evolved prompts ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , or logit-level updates without gradients ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Comparisons of the two disagree, fine-tuning leading on tool tasks ( Alakuijala et al., 2026 ) and the prompt on generalization and on knowledge written in sequence ( Lampinen et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) ; theory ties the answer to the data ( Chan et al., 2025 ) , and recent systems route by volatility ( Ji et al., 2026 ) or run both routes under one budget ( Kim et al., 2026a ) . All of them take a whole trajectory as the unit and change the pipeline with the destination; component routing holds the items fixed and compares the two destinations per component.

sections.heading: Experience forms in GUI agents.
sections.text: GUI agents are trained on trajectories, human demonstrations at first ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026a ) and now their own rollouts in verifiable environments ( Wu et al., 2026j ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . What is kept from a trajectory varies: skills distilled into the weights ( Fan et al., 2026 ) , skill cards retrieved or distilled ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , hindsight-relabelled experience ( Men et al., 2026 ) , and memories built to survive interface change ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . Diagnoses show that trajectory fine-tuning learns interface shortcuts as readily as semantics ( Gu et al., 2026 ) and that a form which helps grounding can hurt action prediction ( Liu et al., 2026b ) . Each of these works fixes one form and one destination. We split one pool into four components and let two measured properties decide where each goes.

sections.heading: Producer, consumer and fragility.
sections.text: Whether self-generated experience helps depends on who produced it and who consumes it ( Ding et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026d ; Duan et al., 2023 ; Fang et al., 2025a ; Fang et al., 2025b ; Fang et al., 2025c ; Pan et al., 2023 ; Tchalla et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Wu et al., 2026f ; Wu et al., 2026g ; Wu et al., 2026h ; Xing et al., 2025 ) : a stronger agent can specialize a smaller one through its weights ( Kim et al., 2026b ) , shared trajectory stores help consumers on either side of the ability gap ( Kim et al., 2026c ) , synthesized tools help only models weaker than their builder ( Lou et al., 2026 ) , and the gain from a harness changes with base ability in opposite directions across studies ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) . Self-improvement loops are also fragile: memory gains move with seeds, task order and backbone ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , much of what a module stores comes from failed or falsely successful runs ( Hajimiri et al., 2026 ; Advani, 2026 ) , and repeated internalization collapses rather than compounds ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . These studies report the net effect of a producer or a consumer. We separate it into an information gap and a policy gap, measured on one pool across three backbone families and a size ladder.

sections.heading: 3 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Figure 3 : Overview. Whole-history reuse (left) against component routing: (A) profile every item of the pool, (B) compare both destinations per component (middle), and reuse each component from its destination on a new task (right). Component routing splits an agent’s own experience into four components and sends each to the context or to the weights of the same agent (Figure 3 ). It treats a trajectory not as one unit but as a bundle of items whose properties can be measured before any route is trained; Appendix A gives the details.

sections.heading: Components.
sections.text: Every item carries a key, a note that the context route serves and a sample that the weights route trains on. A locator says where a named element sits on a screen: its key is application, role and element name, and its sample pairs the screenshot with a click on the element. A procedure is a short run of action targets that recurs inside a task family: its key is three consecutive targets, its note gives the subgoal sequence, and its sample predicts the next action with the subgoals as the thought. A state fact is a precondition that must hold before an action succeeds, extracted from a failed and a successful attempt at the same target: its key is application, target and predicate, and its sample predicts the action with the predicate as the thought. A lesson pairs an action that failed in a state with the one that later succeeded there: its key is application, state and failed target, and its sample is the preference pair. A rule-based extractor produces D c D_{c} .

sections.heading: Two destinations.
sections.text: The context route keeps D c D_{c} in a library indexed by application and key. At a step x x , the items of the same application are ranked by J ⁡ ( x , ⋅ ) J(x,\cdot) against their source states, and the five best are appended to the prompt as notes, exact matches first; the rest of the prompt is the base agent’s, character for character. The weights route fine-tunes the backbone on the samples of the same items with low-rank adaptation ( Hu et al., 2022 , LoRA;) , one configuration for all backbones and arms (Appendix C ), by direct preference optimization ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) for lessons and supervised fine-tuning for the other components; every trained arm reaches a token accuracy of at least 0.90 on a held-in development split. The tuned model is merged and served with the base agent’s prompt, and C c + W c {\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}}{+}{\color[rgb]{0.575,0.4844,0.6531}W_{c}} serves it with the same notes.

sections.heading: Reference arms.
sections.text: Every backbone also runs without experience and with undivided whole trajectories: success-filtered fine-tuning on entire trajectories, retrieval of one similar trajectory, retrieval of ten step-level records by task similarity, and context-then-distill. Three controls probe the instrument: random notes from other applications, notes with shuffled keys and contents, and training samples with shuffled labels. A retry arm keeps the first of three attempts that the agent declares complete, and three aggregate arms send all components to context, all to the weights, or each to the destination the fitted rule assigns (Appendix B ).

sections.heading: Evaluation setup.
sections.text: We evaluate on MobileGym ( Wu et al., 2026j ) and AndroidWorld ( Rawles et al., 2025 ) . MobileGym is a simulated phone with 20 applications and 416 task templates (160 training, 256 test) whose checker compares the application state to the task target; the same state is readable at every step, which makes the keys above well defined. A fixed rank rule holds out 5 applications; the remaining training templates form the pool (122 templates), and the test templates form two held-out tiers, new templates on practiced applications (165) and templates on unseen applications (59), with up to 8 instances per template and seed (1 106 paired instances per seed). AndroidWorld has 116 tasks on 20 real applications and an accessibility tree; 12 applications provide experience, 8 are held out, and 58 held-out tasks are run with four instances each (232 paired instances per seed). Held-out success is decided by each environment’s deterministic checker, with no model judge. Every arm of a backbone is evaluated on the same instances, and differences are read with a paired bootstrap over instances (10 000 resamples, 95 percent intervals), pooled over the two tiers and per tier. Producer and consumer are the same model from three families in the 7–8B range, GUI-Owl-1.5-8B ( Xu et al., 2026 , GUI-Owl-8B below;) , ScaleCUA-7B ( Liu et al., 2026a ) and Qwen3-VL-8B ( Bai et al., 2025 ) ; a same-family ladder, Qwen3-VL 4B, 8B and 32B, serves the producer–consumer measurements. Pool sampling, training and instance sampling are controlled by three seeds, and the analysis of every result was fixed before the runs. Splits, instances and cost are in Appendices B and H.

sections.heading: 4 Observations
sections.text: This section reports what the pool and the two destinations show before any rule is fitted. Every gain is a paired difference on the same held-out instances, with 95 percent intervals from the paired bootstrap. Figure 4 : Components split by destination. (a, b) Route gain Δ ⁡ ( c ) \Delta(c) per backbone on MobileGym and AndroidWorld, with 95 percent intervals; (c) gain of each destination over the base agent, pooled over backbones, one dot per backbone; (d) the pool on the plane of recurrence and state-conditionality, with the component summary of each backbone.

sections.heading: Route gains by component.
sections.text: Figure 4 (a, b) shows the route gain of each component, backbone and environment. Locators are better off in the weights on every backbone and in both environments (+4.9 points pooled over backbones on MobileGym), procedures and state facts are better off in the context ( − - 4.2 and − - 4.1), and lessons lean toward the weights by a margin whose interval includes zero in half of the cells (+1.5). The sign pattern does not depend on the backbone: the twelve MobileGym cells agree across the three families, and the AndroidWorld cells, whose state signature is read from the screen, repeat the pattern with the wider intervals of a smaller task set. Both destinations help every component. Against the base agent and pooled over backbones (Figure 4 c), the context gains between +1.8 and +5.2 points and the weights between +0.8 and +6.7; what differs is which route helps more, the weights for locators (+6.7 against +1.8) and the context for procedures (+5.2 against +1.0). Coexistence adds little where the weights already win. Serving the notes on top of the tuned model adds +0.1 points for locators and +3.5 for state facts, so the context remains useful exactly for the components that the context wins. The components differ before any training. Figure 4 (d) places the items on the plane of the two properties. Procedures almost never recur outside their task family (mean recurrence 0.05) and are state-conditioned (0.66); locators recur (0.39) and are nearly state-free (0.10); state facts and lessons recur (0.32 and 0.45) and are state-conditioned (0.56 and 0.53). The three backbones place every component in the same region of the plane. Observation 1. Split by component, one pool has opposite winning destinations: locators, and weakly lessons, in the weights; procedures and state facts in the context; on three backbone families and two environments.

sections.heading: 4.2 Producer and Consumer
sections.text: Figure 5 : Producer and consumer. (a) Gain from the procedures of a producer of each size, read from the context (solid) or written into the weights (dashed); filled markers train on the consumer’s own procedures only. (b) One consumer, five producers, three destinations.

sections.heading: Producers and consumers.
sections.text: Figure 5 (a) follows the Qwen3-VL family across sizes, in a batch where every procedures adapter trains on the same number of samples (Appendix B.1 ). Procedures read from the context help every consumer whoever produced them, and larger producers help more: the 8B consumer gains +3.6 points from its own procedures, +4.8 from those of the 32B model and +2.2 from those of the 4B model, and the 32B consumer still gains +3.2 from the procedures of the 8B model. The same items written into the weights follow a different rule. Fine-tuning the 8B consumer on the procedures of the 4B model changes it by − - 2.3 points, on those of the 32B model by − - 1.4, and on those of another family by − - 7.5 (Figure 5 b), while its own procedures give +0.9. The damage is policy mismatch, not information. The same other-family pool read from the context gives +3.6, and a producer of the other family retrained on the consumer’s own successes brings the weights route back to − - 2.0. Most of the weights gain on own procedures is practice. Fine-tuning on the consumer’s own procedures alone, without any transferred item, gives +0.6 against +0.9 with all samples, and the two agree within 1.1 points on all five consumers (Figure 5 a, filled markers), so the weights route pays for what the consumer already does more than for what it learns. Observation 2. Notes help regardless of who produced them, and more so from a stronger producer; fine-tuning helps only when producer and consumer are the same model, and most of its gain is practice on the consumer’s own trajectories.

sections.heading: 4.3 Readout after Training
sections.text: Figure 6 : Readout after training. (a) Share of probed steps whose action changes after a note is read, before and after the same items are in the weights; (b) the after-to-before ratio against the component’s recurrence.

sections.heading: Readout probe.
sections.text: The readout probe replays a decision step with and without a retrieved note and records whether the action changes. Before training, a note changes the action in 42 percent of the probed steps, from 33 percent for procedures to 48 percent for lessons, at about the same rate on every consumer (Figure 6 a). After the same items are in the weights, the rate falls to 16 percent for locators and 15 percent for lessons but only to 22 percent for procedures, and the after-to-before ratio falls with the recurrence of the component (Figure 6 b, Spearman − - 0.92). The same holds among the items of one component: split into thirds by recurrence, the ratio falls from 0.73 to 0.11 for locators and from 0.63 to 0.11 for lessons (Table E.4 ). Redundancy rather than conflict. The drop is largest for lessons and locators, the two components that recur most and for which coexistence added the least above, and smallest for procedures, the component for which the context keeps its value after training. A note is read when it carries something the weights do not yet hold, and a component that recurs is the one the weights absorb. Observation 3. Training on a component makes its notes redundant, and the more the component recurs, the less its notes are read afterwards.

sections.heading: 5 The Routing Rule
sections.text: This section fits a rule in the two pool measurements, tests it on held-out backbone families, and examines interventions, training and version changes.

sections.heading: Held-out fit.
sections.text: Each component has one destination across backbone families, and a linear rule in the two properties recovers it on a family it has not seen. We score a component by its recurrence against its state-conditionality and fit the score to the sign of the route gain, holding out one family at a time. sections.heading: One property at a time.
sections.text: Changing one property moves a component the way the rule says. Table 1 reports the arms that change one property of a component, with the shift from the unmodified route in its last column. A larger training dose moves procedures toward the weights. A key that recurs in more tasks contributes more samples to the weights route, so recurrence reaches the weights as the number of updates a key receives. Copying every procedure item eightfold before fine-tuning reproduces that dose and changes no item: it moves the route gain of procedures from − - 4.2 to − - 0.8, across zero on Qwen3-VL-8B (+1.0). Read as recurrence, eight copies place procedures at r ≈ 0.42 r\approx 0.42{} , short of the boundary at their state-conditionality ( r ≈ 0.44 r\approx 0.44{} ), and the route gain stays below zero on average. State facts move by +3.6 and reach the context route on Qwen3-VL-8B , and with two and four copies the gain grows with the dose (Table E.1 ). At ten times the learning rate the weights route changes by +1.0 and +1.0 points, and the route gains of procedures and state facts stay at − - 3.3 and − - 3.2. Removing the state condition removes most of the context gain. Serving the same notes retrieved by task text alone, without their state condition, costs 3.4 points for state facts and 3.9 for procedures, so what the context route buys for these two components is the condition, not the payload. Reading the condition from the visible screen elements instead of the environment state keeps most of it: the notes lose 0.7 points for procedures and 0.7 for state facts, and both stay in the context (route gains − - 3.5 and − - 3.5). Shuffled items do nothing. Shuffling the keys of the notes or of the training samples leaves the base agent within 1.1 points (Table E.1 ), and random notes from other applications change it by − - 1.6; neither the prompt format nor the fine-tuning itself produces the gains.

sections.heading: Stale weights, fresh notes.
sections.text: When the weights and the context disagree, the more an item recurs, the less often the agent follows the note and the more often it takes neither action. To see what happens when the two disagree, we train the weights on version 1 of the OpenApps applications ( Ullrich et al., 2026 ) , serve notes from version 2, and record, at the first step of a task where the two versions call for different actions, whether the agent follows the note, the weights or neither (Figure 8 , bottom, shows one such step). On the new version, stale weights alone change the base agent by − - 8.4 points and fresh notes alone by +3.3; serving both scores between 2.7 and 12.7 points below notes alone. Recurrence shifts the outcome. At the divergence step the agent follows the note in 52 percent of the low-recurrence cases and 43 percent of the high-recurrence ones, the weights in 34 percent and 21 percent, and neither in 14 percent and 36 percent. This is the readout result from the other side: the items the weights hold best are the items a contradicting note corrects least, and when the weights hold a stale version of such an item, the agent more often takes neither action.

sections.heading: Against the alternatives.
sections.text: Routing by the held-out rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline and, on average over backbones, the better single destination. Table 2 compares them on the same held-out instances, with the gain of routing over each row on MobileGym in its last column (compute and tokens in Appendix H ). Routed sends each component where the held-out rule says, so its assignment on a backbone is fixed before that backbone is trained. Fitted on one half of the held-out templates instead, the rule gives the same assignment in five of the six folds, and routing leads the better single destination on the other half by +3.7 to +5.1 points on MobileGym and +2.4 to +2.6 on AndroidWorld (Table D.3 ). On the full set it exceeds the better single destination on every MobileGym backbone, by +4.4 points on average; on AndroidWorld it exceeds it by +5.0 with Qwen3-VL-8B and by +3.2 with ScaleCUA-7B , and matches it with GUI-Owl-8B . The single destinations fail on different components. All to the context forgoes the weights gain of locators, all to the weights the context gain of procedures and state facts; routing keeps both (Figure 8 , top). Components carry what whole trajectories do not. The best whole-trajectory baseline, three sampled attempts with self-retry, is +9.3 points below routing, and fine-tuning on whole trajectories, retrieval of one trajectory or of ten step records, and context-then-distill all stay below the single destinations. The lead comes from what the components extract: localization samples for locators, preference pairs drawn from failed attempts for lessons, and notes matched to the current state for procedures and state facts. Without the state match, the notes of procedures and state facts gain +1.3 and +1.6, as ten step records retrieved by task text do (+1.4); retrieved by the state signature instead, the same records gain +1.6 (Table E.1 ), still 3.6 and 3.4 points below the notes of procedures and state facts. Fine-tuning on whole trajectories gains +0.7, about as much as procedures in the weights (+1.0). The assignment is what matters. The reverse assignment loses +8.9 points against routing on MobileGym and +6.7 on AndroidWorld, and the in-sample rule assigns the same routes, so routing by the full fit differs by − - 0.2.

sections.heading: Along the ladder.
sections.text: A larger producer widens the information gap, a foreign one opens a policy gap, and each route follows its own. For the Qwen3-VL-8B consumer, the 4B, 8B and 32B producers of its family have information gaps of 0.04, 0.06 and 0.08 and the same policy gap (0.16); their notes gain more in that order, and in the weights only the consumer’s own samples gain (Figure 5 a), the practice term of Equation 6 . A foreign producer is a policy gap, not an information gap. The GUI-Owl-8B pool has the information gap of a same-family producer (0.07) and a policy gap of 0.46: its notes help as much as the consumer’s own, and its samples hurt (Figure 5 b). Retraining that producer on the consumer’s successes closes the policy gap (0.17), leaves the information gap (0.07), and brings its samples to what a same-family producer’s give.

sections.heading: Consumer upgrade.
sections.text: After an upgrade the notes keep their value and the weights start over, because what the weights bought was practice. When the consumer moves from the 8B to the 32B model of the same family, the notes of the 8B producer still give the 32B consumer +3.2 points and the same samples in its weights − - 1.4. Practice needs no producer. On all five consumers, fine-tuning on the consumer’s own successes alone, from families it already solves, matches its full procedures within 1.1 points (Figure 9 d). A note library therefore carries over a change of consumer, and the weights route is rebuilt from the new consumer’s own trajectories.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented component routing, which sends each component of a GUI agent’s own experience to the context or to the weights by two properties measured on the pool before any training, recurrence and state-conditionality. On the same items and held-out tasks across three backbone families and two environments, one pool has two destinations: locators and lessons win in the weights, procedures and state facts in the context. A rule in the two properties recovers the destination of every component on a held-out family and of both halves of a component split at its boundary, and routing by it beats every whole-trajectory baseline and, on average, the better single destination of each backbone. Note readout falls once the same component is in the weights, most for the components that recur most; context gains grow with the information gap and weights gains shrink with the policy gap, so where experience belongs also depends on who produced it and who consumes it.

sections.heading: Appendix A Components and Items
sections.text: An item is one unit of experience taken from the pool: a key that identifies it across episodes, a payload that the route carries, and a state condition under which the payload applies. The four cards below give the three fields of each component together with the note the context route serves and the training sample the weights route trains on, as defined in Section 3 . The example on each card is one item of a GUI-Owl-8B pool as its note, in the template of Appendix I.3 , with an English rendering. Table A.1 counts the items per component and environment, and Figure A.1 shows the item-level distributions behind it. Figure A.1 : Pool statistics. (a) Items per pool by component and backbone on MobileGym (dark) and AndroidWorld (light), mean over seeds with the seed range. (b) Distribution of item recurrence and (c) of state-conditionality over the items that have one, per component; MobileGym solid, AndroidWorld dashed.

sections.heading: A.1 Component Cards
sections.text: Component Card: Locators ( G ) Description: where a named element sits on a screen. Key: (application, role, element name). Payload: the position of the element on that screen. State condition: the screen on which the element was found. As a note: one line that names the element and its position, served when the current screen matches the key. As a training sample: the screenshot paired with a click on the element. Example item: 在 weather 的该页面上，元素「城市管理」（div）的点击坐标是 (770, 84)。 On this page of weather, the element “City management” (div) is tapped at (770, 84). Key (weather, div, City management); payload (770, 84). Component Card: Procedures ( P ) Description: a short run of action targets that recurs inside a task family. Key: the run of three consecutive targets. Payload: the subgoal sequence of the run. State condition: the task family and the screen at which the run starts. As a note: a hint that lists the subgoals in order, served when the task and the screen match the key. As a training sample: task, screenshot and history mapped to the next action, with the subgoals as the thought. Example item: 在 weather 中，做完「城市管理」「深圳市」后，下一步通常是「如：一般」。 In weather, after “City management” and “Shenzhen”, the next step is usually “e.g. Fair”. Key (City management, Shenzhen, e.g. Fair); payload: the third target. Component Card: State facts ( F ) Description: a precondition that must hold before an action succeeds, taken from a failed and a successful attempt at the same target. Key: (application, target, predicate). Payload: the predicate. State condition: the screen that shows the target. As a note: one line that states the precondition, served when the target is on the current screen. As a training sample: the source step mapped to the action, with the predicate as the thought. Example item: 在 answer_sheet 中执行「提交答案」之前，需要满足：apps.answer_sheet.answers.0 须为任务要求的值。 Before doing “Submit answer” in answer_sheet, the following must hold: apps.answer_sheet.answers.0 must be the value the task requires. Key (answer_sheet, Submit answer, answers.0 set to the required value); payload: the predicate. Component Card: Lessons ( L ) Description: an action that failed in a state, paired with the action that later succeeded there. Key: (application, state, failed target). Payload: the action that succeeded. State condition: the state in which the failed action was taken. As a note: one line that names the failed action and the one that succeeded, served when the state matches the key. As a training sample: the preference pair at the source state, the succeeded action chosen and the failed action rejected. Example item: 在 answer_sheet 的该状态下不要执行「如：一般」，应执行「提交答案」。 In this state of answer_sheet, do not do “e.g. Fair”; do “Submit answer” instead. Key (answer_sheet, the source state, e.g. Fair); payload: Submit answer.

sections.heading: Appendix B Arms and Protocol
sections.text: This appendix gives the design constants behind Section 3 : the two environments and their splits, the pools, every arm, and the interaction budget. All of them were fixed before the runs; measured outcomes are in the main text and in Appendix E .

sections.heading: MobileGym.
sections.text: MobileGym has 20 applications and 416 task templates in 24 suites, split by the benchmark into 160 training and 256 test templates. A template instantiates a task with sampled parameters, and the environment judges an episode by comparing the final application state with the target state. Applications are ranked by their number of training templates, and every fourth application in that ranking is held out as unseen; this gives 5 unseen applications. Training templates whose applications are all seen form the experience pool (122 templates). Test templates whose applications are all seen form the seen split (165), test templates whose applications are all unseen form the unseen split (59), and the 32 test templates that touch both are reported separately and enter no main-text number. Each held-out template is instantiated up to 8 times per seed (126 templates have 8 instances and 98 have one), with parameters fixed by (template, instance, seed) and stored, so every arm runs the same 1 106 instances per seed.

sections.heading: AndroidWorld.
sections.text: AndroidWorld has 116 tasks over 20 applications, judged by the official evaluator. The unseen tier takes 8 of the 20 applications (identifiers audiorec , draw , joplin , notes , osmand , retro , simplecal and vlc ). The 58 held-out tasks are instantiated four times per seed, 232 instances, and the remaining tasks form the pool. The state signature is the set of visible accessibility nodes (class, resource id, normalized text), capped at 500 nodes, together with the package and activity. Locator keys are (application, class, resource id or text); procedure keys are three consecutive action-target signatures; state-fact keys are the node signatures present in the successful state and absent in the failed one, at most five; lesson keys are as on MobileGym. Actions follow the official action space through each backbone’s own adapter.

sections.heading: Pools.
sections.text: On MobileGym the base agent of each family runs every experience template 20 times at temperature 1 with a fresh instance each time, once per seed. Every step records the screenshot, the environment state, the element list, the action and its target. On AndroidWorld the pool runs each pool task ten times. The four component extractors run on the pool once, and the recurrence and state-conditionality of every item are computed from the pool alone. The coordinates of a cell are the mean recurrence and the median state-conditionality over the items of its component, merged over the three seeds. For the producer ladder of Section 6 the pools are repeated with the 4B and 32B members of the Qwen3-VL family and the 32B member of the GUI-Owl family as producers.

sections.heading: Producer–consumer batch.
sections.text: The measurements of Sections 4.2 and 6 come from one batch of their own. Every procedures adapter of this batch trains on 5 600 samples drawn from the producer’s pool (1 900 for the 32B consumers), so every producer enters the weights at the same training budget, and its own-procedure arms are separate runs from those of Table 1 . The batch groups the held-out templates into 16 task families: eight single-application suites, three cross-application suites and five kinds of task shared across applications (search and filter, compose and send, settings toggles, media control and multi-step forms).

sections.heading: Version change.
sections.text: The conflict measurement of Section 5.3 uses OpenApps ( Ullrich et al., 2026 ) , whose 15 tasks over six applications exist in two application versions. Each version is sampled 20 times per task. The weights route is trained on version 1 items, the notes are served from version 2, and every arm runs on all three families and three seeds, on 150 version-2 instances per seed (ten goal variants per task). At the first state where the two versions’ successful procedures diverge, the arm’s action is compared with the version-2 note and with the version-1 weights without notes, under the same-action rule of Appendix B.3 ; the shares of Section 5.3 count 520 such steps, 312 on GUI-Owl-8B and 104 on each other family.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: All arms use greedy decoding, the official step limit, the native screen resolution, and the same stored instances. An episode is a success when the environment judge accepts the final state. Every reported difference between two arms is paired over (template, instance, seed) and carries a percentile interval from 10 000 bootstrap resamples of the paired differences. Cells pool the three seeds; per-seed values give the subscripts of the tables.

sections.heading: B.2 Arms
sections.text: The arm names below are the ones of the delivered result tables. Unless stated, an arm runs on all three families, both environments and all seeds. Base agent and single-component routes: • none : the base agent with the evaluation prompt and no experience; the zero of every gain. • C_G, C_P, C_F, C_L : the context route of one component. At every step the items of the same application are ranked by the Jaccard similarity of their source state signature to the current one. Exact matches (at least 0.9) come first and relaxed matches (at least 0.5) fill up to five notes, appended to the prompt as a notes block. Procedures retrieve the skill file of the most similar task text first and the step-level items within it second. • C_c_exact, C_c_relaxed : the context route restricted to the exact or to the relaxed tier; their difference against none gives the online state-conditionality of Equation 4 . • W_G, W_P, W_F : the weights route of one component, a LoRA adapter fine-tuned on the component’s items rendered as samples (Appendix C ). W_L trains the adapter by preference optimization, with the successful action as chosen and the failed action as rejected. • CW_G, CW_P, CW_F, CW_L : the weights-route adapter served with the notes of the same component. Every note-bearing step also runs once without the note, which gives the after-training readout of Section 4.3 . Aggregate arms: • all_C : the four libraries served together, at most two notes per component and eight in total, exact matches first. • all_W : one adapter trained on the locator, procedure and state-fact samples together, then preference-optimized on the lessons from that adapter. • routed : each component sent where the rule fitted with the family held out says (Appendix D ). The components sent to the weights are trained as in all_W restricted to those components; the components sent to the context are served with the all_C quota. The assignment is written to disk before the adapter is trained. • anti_routed : the same with every destination reversed. • routed_self : the destinations read from the family’s own observed signs, used as an in-sample routing reference; GUI-Owl-8B only. sections.heading: B.3 Interaction Budget
sections.text: All arms use the same held-out instances and the official per-episode step limit. Each arm runs one episode per instance, except self-retry, which runs three attempts. The two routes consume the same items: the notes and the training samples of a component are rendered from the same extracted items of the same pool. Two quantities the budget does not equalize are reported in Appendix H : the notes block that the context route adds to every prompt, and the adapter training run that the weights route adds. Two actions count as the same when they are of the same type and, for taps, hit the same element or land within 2 percent of the screen diagonal of each other; for text entry, carry the same stripped text; for scrolls, go in the same direction. This rule decides the readout of Section 4.3 , the policy gap of Section 6 and the conflict outcome of Section 5.3 .

sections.heading: Appendix C Training Setup
sections.text: Every weights-route arm is a LoRA adapter trained on the base agent of its family and merged before serving. The vision tower stays frozen, and a weights-route arm is evaluated with the prompt of the base agent, without a notes block. Every adapter of every family uses the same configuration, fixed before the runs: rank 16, α \alpha 32, three epochs, learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} . Table C.1 lists the samples of every adapter and its token accuracy on a held-in tenth of them.

sections.heading: Samples.
sections.text: A locator item becomes one sample per source step: the screenshot and the instruction to tap the named element, with the tap coordinates as the target. A procedure item becomes the step-by-step samples of the successful trajectories of its task family, with the sub-goal sequence as the thought. A state-fact item becomes its source step, task, screenshot and history, with the predicate as the thought and the action as the target. A lesson item becomes a preference pair on its source state, the successful action as chosen and the failed action as rejected, trained by preference optimization from the same adapter configuration. Success-filtered fine-tuning takes every step of every successful pool episode; context-then-distill takes the successful teacher episodes of the context route, at the sample count of the weights route of the same component; the copy interventions repeat the source episodes of a component before extraction, so their sample counts are the multiples listed in the table.

sections.heading: C.2 Context Route
sections.text: The notes of a component are its items rendered as one line each in a fixed template. A locator note names the element, its role and its position; a procedure note gives the sub-goal sequence of its skill file and the next sub-goal; a state-fact note states the condition that must hold before its action; a lesson note names the action to avoid in its state and the action to take instead. At every step the library of the current application is ranked by the Jaccard similarity between each item’s source state signature and the current signature, exact matches (at least 0.9) before relaxed matches (at least 0.5). The top five notes are appended to the prompt as a notes block, and the rest of the prompt is the base agent’s. Procedures are retrieved in two stages: the skill file of the most similar task text, then the step-level items within it. The aggregate context arms serve at most two notes per component and eight in total, exact matches first. Prompt tokens are recorded with and without the notes block on every step and enter Appendix H .

sections.heading: Matching thresholds.
sections.text: The exact and relaxed tiers of the context route move from 0.9 and 0.5 to 0.8 and 0.6, for all four components.

sections.heading: Notes per step.
sections.text: The context route of locators and state facts serves three or ten notes instead of five.

sections.heading: Adapter rank.
sections.text: The weights route of locators and state facts is trained at rank 64 and 128 instead of 16, at the same number of epochs.

sections.heading: Pool size.

sections.heading: Library cap.

You are an expert operator of a mobile GUI agent. Given the task, the current screenshot and the history of operations, analyse the screen and output one action to interact with the phone and complete the task. Coordinates have their origin at the top left, x x to the right and y y downward, both in the range 0 to 1000. The fifteen actions, in JSON, are click, double tap, long press, type (with an optional point and an optional clear flag), swipe, drag, back, home, recent apps, enter, wait, open app, submit an answer, complete the task with a short note, and abort with a reason. The output is a <THINK> block that states what the screen shows, what to do next and which element to operate, followed by an <ANSWER> block with one JSON action. Coordinates must be numbers in 0 to 1000, the JSON must be valid, decisions follow the screenshot, questions are answered with the answer action, and the complete action is used only after the task has been carried out.

sections.heading: I.2 User Turn
sections.text: The user turn of a step carries the current screenshot and, on the first step of the history window, the instruction text below with the task and the summary of previous actions filled in. GUI-Owl-1.5-8B keeps a window of the last four steps, each as its screenshot followed by the full model output of that step, and lists older steps as one line each; ScaleCUA-7B sends the current screenshot with a one-line history; Qwen3-VL-8B keeps its previous outputs as text and sends the screenshot of the current step only. A weights-route arm and the base agent receive exactly these messages. A context-route arm receives the same messages plus one text part appended after the current screenshot, the notes block of Appendix I.3 , and nothing is appended on a step without retrieved items. For the readout probe of Section 4.3 , every step that received a notes block is also run once without it; both outputs are logged, and the action with the block is the one executed. Instruction: {task} Previous actions: {previous_actions} Instruction text of the user turn, ScaleCUA-7B Please generate the next move according to the UI screenshot, the task and previous operations. The first turn is the line “[Task]” followed by the task; later turns are “[Step i i ]” followed by the current screenshot.

sections.heading: I.3 Notes Block
sections.text: The block is one text part with a fixed header and one line per retrieved item, in retrieval order; the aggregate arms list the components in the order locators, procedures, state facts, lessons. Two headers exist, one per coordinate frame. Notes block, GUI-Owl-1.5-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B (0–1000 frame) [经验笔记]（来自过去在同一应用上的使用经验，仅供参考；坐标与截图同为 0–1000 尺度；以当前截图和任务为 ↪ \hookrightarrow 准） {notes} Notes block, ScaleCUA-7B (952 x 2156 frame) [经验笔记]（来自过去在同一应用上的使用经验，仅供参考；坐标为模型看到的截图像素坐标（952 × 2156）；以 ↪ \hookrightarrow 当前截图和任务为准） {notes} English rendering of the header. “[Experience notes] (from past use of the same application, for reference only; coordinates are on the same 0 to 1000 scale as the screenshot; the current screenshot and task take precedence)”. The ScaleCUA header states instead that coordinates are in the pixel frame the model sees, 952 by 2156. Item templates, one line per item G 在 {app} 的该页面上，元素「{name}」（{role}）的点击坐标是 ({x}, {y})。 P 在 {app} 中，做完「{name1}」「{name2}」后，下一步通常是「{name3}」。 F 在 {app} 中执行「{name}」之前，需要满足：{pred1}；{pred2}；…。 L 在 {app} 的该状态下不要执行「{name_fail}」，应执行「{name_success}」。 English rendering of the templates. A locator note reads “On this page of {app}, the element ‘{name}’ ({role}) is tapped at ({x}, {y})”. A procedure note reads “In {app}, after ‘{name1}’ and ‘{name2}’, the next step is usually ‘{name3}”’. A state-fact note reads “Before doing ‘{name}’ in {app}, the following must hold: {pred1}; {pred2}; …”, with at most five predicates. A lesson note reads “In this state of {app}, do not do ‘{name_fail}’; do ‘{name_success}’ instead”. A predicate is one of three forms over a path of the application state, with list identifiers replaced by a placeholder: “{path} exists”, “{path} is set (non-empty)”, or “{path} must be the value the task requires”; keys that change on every run, such as timestamps and identifiers, never enter a predicate. text: Not All Experience Belongs in the Weights: Component Routing for Self-Improving GUI Agents Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: arXiv is now an independent nonprofit! Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.01787v1 [cs.AI] 01 Oct 2026 Not All Experience Belongs in the Weights: Component Routing for Self-Improving GUI Agents Beining Wu Wu.Beining@jacks.sdstate.edu Affiliation: Zihao Ding Zihao.Ding@jacks.sdstate.edu Affiliation: Jun Huang Jun.Huang@sdstate.edu Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, South Dakota State University Abstract Self-improving GUI agents keep the trajectories they produce and return them to the agent, by fine-tuning or by retrieval into the prompt, and studies that compare the two destinations disagree. We attribute this to the unit of experience: a trajectory bundles items with different properties, so a conclusion about the bundle depends on its mix. To address this, (i) we introduce component routing , which splits the experience into locators, procedures, state facts and lessons and sends each component to the context or to the weights, compared on the same items across three backbone families, two environments and three seeds. One pool has two destinations: locators and lessons win in the weights, procedures and state facts in the context. (ii) We fit a rule in two properties measured before any training, recurrence and state-conditionality; it recovers the destination of a held-out backbone family in 24 of 24 cells, two interventions move a component toward the boundary, and routing by the rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline and, by +3.5 points on average, the better single destination of each backbone. (iii) We identify how training and producer–consumer differences change the value of the two destinations: note readout decreases after the same component is written into the weights, most for the items that recur most, context gains increase with the information gap, and weights gains decrease with the policy gap. Code and data will be released. Figure 1 : Component routing. (a) The four components on the plane of recurrence r r and state-conditionality κ \kappa , measured before any training; fill marks the winning destination on held-out tasks, the dashed line is the fitted boundary, the arrow one intervention. (b) Held-out success, mean over three backbones and three seeds; arrows: gain over whole-trajectory fine-tuning and the higher single-destination bar. 1 Introduction GUI agents that operate phones and desktops are increasingly improved with their own traces: an agent runs a batch of tasks, the trajectories are kept, and the experience is returned to the agent. Figure 2 : A motivating example. G recurs across tasks and goes to the weights; P matters only on the preview screen and stays in context. Screens are illustrative. Where that experience should go is an open decision. One line of work fine-tunes the agent on its successful trajectories; another keeps the trajectories, or notes distilled from them, in a library that is retrieved into the prompt. On MobileGym, an 8B agent whose whole pool goes to the weights gains 7.1 points of held-out success and one whose whole pool goes to the context gains 8.0, yet the two destinations disagree on which parts of the pool are responsible: the components that gain most in the weights are the ones that gain least in context (Figure 1 a). Figure 2 shows the smallest version of this. One trajectory on a weather application teaches where the search field is and that a city is saved by tapping Add on its preview; fine-tuning on the whole trajectory learns the first and loses the second. We attribute this to the unit of experience. Existing methods treat a trajectory as the unit: success-filtered fine-tuning distills whole trajectories into the weights ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Men et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) , and retrieval keeps whole trajectories or trajectory-level skills in context ( Xiong et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Sui et al., 2026 ) . Comparisons of the two destinations reach opposite conclusions: internalized hints beat the prompt on tool tasks ( Alakuijala et al., 2026 ) , prompt-side updates beat gradient updates on web tasks ( Li et al., 2026 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , and the same skill representation helps one task and hurts another ( Liu et al., 2026b ) . A trajectory bundles items with different properties, so any conclusion about the bundle depends on its mix. Deciding where a piece of experience belongs requires two things: a property of the piece that can be measured before any training, and a comparison in which both destinations consume the same items and are read on the same held-out tasks. Existing comparisons pit one whole pipeline against another, so the items differ before the destinations do ( Alakuijala et al., 2026 ; Gou et al., 2026 ) , and none asks it per component. Core question Which components of an agent’s own experience belong in its context and which in its weights, and does the answer survive training and a change of backbone? We answer this question with component routing . Experience is split into four components, locators, procedures, state facts and lessons, and each component is characterized by two properties measured on the pool before any training: recurrence , how often its key comes up in unrelated tasks, and state-conditionality , how much its usefulness depends on the current state matching its source state. Each component is then sent to the context, to the weights, or to both, on the same items and the same held-out instances, across three backbone families and two environments. Three observations follow. The four components split by destination: the route gain, weights minus context, is +4.9 points for locators and +1.5 for lessons, − - 4.2 for procedures and − - 4.1 for state facts (Figure 1 a). The two properties account for the split: a rule fitted with the tested backbone held out recovers the sign in 24 of 24 cells, an eightfold training dose moves procedures toward the weights by +3.5 points, and stripping the state condition from state facts costs 3.4. Routing each component by the rule exceeds the better single destination of each backbone by +3.5 points on average over three backbones and two environments, and the reverse assignment by +7.8 (Figure 1 b). Contributions. (i) A measurement of where an agent’s own experience belongs: four components, two pool-level properties, and a paired comparison of the context and the weights on the same items across three backbones, two environments and three seeds. (ii) A routing rule in recurrence and state-conditionality that recovers the winning destination of every component on a held-out backbone family, with two interventions that move a component toward the boundary. (iii) An account of how training, information gaps and policy gaps shape experience reuse: the readout of high-recurrence notes falls to 16 percent once the same items are in the weights, most for the items that recur most, and the context route gains from an information gap while the weights route loses to a policy gap. 2 Related Work Two destinations for experience. Self-improving agents return their own experience along two routes. Fine-tuning writes it into the weights ( Ding & Huang, 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026b ; Ding et al., 2026c ; Wu & Huang, 2026b ; Wu et al., 2026c ; Wu et al., 2026d ; Wu et al., 2026i ) , on the agent’s rollouts ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Men et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026a ; Huang et al., 2025a ; Huang et al., 2025b ; Wu & Wu, 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , on skills extracted from them ( Fan et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026k ) , or by distilling a helpful context into the parameters ( Alakuijala et al., 2026 ; Gou et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Retrieval keeps it in a store that is read into the prompt ( Wu & Huang, 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026e ) : trajectory and skill libraries ( Xiong et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) , evolved prompts ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , or logit-level updates without gradients ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Comparisons of the two disagree, fine-tuning leading on tool tasks ( Alakuijala et al., 2026 ) and the prompt on generalization and on knowledge written in sequence ( Lampinen et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) ; theory ties the answer to the data ( Chan et al., 2025 ) , and recent systems route by volatility ( Ji et al., 2026 ) or run both routes under one budget ( Kim et al., 2026a ) . All of them take a whole trajectory as the unit and change the pipeline with the destination; component routing holds the items fixed and compares the two destinations per component. Experience forms in GUI agents. GUI agents are trained on trajectories, human demonstrations at first ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026a ) and now their own rollouts in verifiable environments ( Wu et al., 2026j ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . What is kept from a trajectory varies: skills distilled into the weights ( Fan et al., 2026 ) , skill cards retrieved or distilled ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , hindsight-relabelled experience ( Men et al., 2026 ) , and memories built to survive interface change ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . Diagnoses show that trajectory fine-tuning learns interface shortcuts as readily as semantics ( Gu et al., 2026 ) and that a form which helps grounding can hurt action prediction ( Liu et al., 2026b ) . Each of these works fixes one form and one destination. We split one pool into four components and let two measured properties decide where each goes. Producer, consumer and fragility. Whether self-generated experience helps depends on who produced it and who consumes it ( Ding et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026d ; Duan et al., 2023 ; Fang et al., 2025a ; Fang et al., 2025b ; Fang et al., 2025c ; Pan et al., 2023 ; Tchalla et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Wu et al., 2026f ; Wu et al., 2026g ; Wu et al., 2026h ; Xing et al., 2025 ) : a stronger agent can specialize a smaller one through its weights ( Kim et al., 2026b ) , shared trajectory stores help consumers on either side of the ability gap ( Kim et al., 2026c ) , synthesized tools help only models weaker than their builder ( Lou et al., 2026 ) , and the gain from a harness changes with base ability in opposite directions across studies ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) . Self-improvement loops are also fragile: memory gains move with seeds, task order and backbone ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , much of what a module stores comes from failed or falsely successful runs ( Hajimiri et al., 2026 ; Advani, 2026 ) , and repeated internalization collapses rather than compounds ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . These studies report the net effect of a producer or a consumer. We separate it into an information gap and a policy gap, measured on one pool across three backbone families and a size ladder. 3 Experimental Setup Figure 3 : Overview. Whole-history reuse (left) against component routing: (A) profile every item of the pool, (B) compare both destinations per component (middle), and reuse each component from its destination on a new task (right). Component routing splits an agent’s own experience into four components and sends each to the context or to the weights of the same agent (Figure 3 ). It treats a trajectory not as one unit but as a bundle of items whose properties can be measured before any route is trained; Appendix A gives the details. Problem formulation. An agent with policy π \pi runs a batch of tasks on a fixed set of applications and keeps every trajectory, successful or not; each step records the screenshot, the structured application state, the on-screen elements, and the action with its target element. This batch is the experience pool E E . An extractor maps E E to four item sets D c D_{c} , c ∈ { G , P , F , L } c\in\{G,P,F,L\} , where G G , P P , F F and L L denote locators, procedures, state facts and lessons, and every item d ∈ D c d\in D_{c} carries a key k ⁡ ( d ) k(d) that identifies it across episodes. A destination turns an item set into a policy: the context route C c {\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}} retrieves items of D c D_{c} into the prompt at each step, the weights route W c {\color[rgb]{0.575,0.4844,0.6531}W_{c}} fine-tunes π \pi on them, and the coexistence arm C c + W c {\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}}{+}{\color[rgb]{0.575,0.4844,0.6531}W_{c}} does both. Let T T be the set of held-out task instances and u ⁡ ( x , ρ ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } u(x;\rho)\in\{0,1\} the checker’s verdict on instance x x under policy ρ \rho , so that U ⁡ ( ρ ) = | T | − 1 ​ ∑ x ∈ T u ⁡ ( x , ρ ) U(\rho)=|T|^{-1}\sum_{x\in T}u(x;\rho) is held-out success. The quantity this paper measures is the route gain Δ ⁡ ( c ) \displaystyle\Delta(c) ≜ U ⁡ ( W c ) − U ⁡ ( C c ) \displaystyle\triangleq\;\hbox{\pagecolor{AccentW!45}$\displaystyle U({\color[rgb]{0.575,0.4844,0.6531}W_{c}})$}\;-\;\hbox{\pagecolor{AccentC!40}$\displaystyle U({\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}})$} (1) = 1 | T | ​ ∑ x ∈ T [ u ⁡ ( x , W c ) − u ⁡ ( x , C c ) ] , ⊳ one paired comparison per instance \displaystyle=\;\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{x\in T}\Bigl[\;\hbox{\pagecolor{AccentW!45}$\displaystyle u\bigl(x;{\color[rgb]{0.575,0.4844,0.6531}W_{c}}\bigr)$}\;-\;\hbox{\pagecolor{AccentC!40}$\displaystyle u\bigl(x;{\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}}\bigr)$}\;\Bigr],\qquad{\color[rgb]{0.35,0.35,0.35}\text{\scriptsize$\triangleright$\,one paired comparison per instance}} where Δ ⁡ ( c ) > 0 \Delta(c)>0 means that component c c is better off in the weights. Components. Every item carries a key, a note that the context route serves and a sample that the weights route trains on. A locator says where a named element sits on a screen: its key is application, role and element name, and its sample pairs the screenshot with a click on the element. A procedure is a short run of action targets that recurs inside a task family: its key is three consecutive targets, its note gives the subgoal sequence, and its sample predicts the next action with the subgoals as the thought. A state fact is a precondition that must hold before an action succeeds, extracted from a failed and a successful attempt at the same target: its key is application, target and predicate, and its sample predicts the action with the predicate as the thought. A lesson pairs an action that failed in a state with the one that later succeeded there: its key is application, state and failed target, and its sample is the preference pair. A rule-based extractor produces D c D_{c} . State signature. The state at a step x x is summarized by a signature S ⁡ ( x ) S(x) , the application route together with the set of path–value pairs of the environment state without volatile fields such as timestamps; on AndroidWorld, whose application state is not exposed, the signature is the set of visible accessibility nodes, the view a deployed agent has (Appendix B.1 ). Steps of one application are compared by the Jaccard similarity J ⁡ ( x , y ) = | S ⁡ ( x ) ∩ S ⁡ ( y ) | / | S ⁡ ( x ) ∪ S ⁡ ( y ) | J(x,y)=|S(x)\cap S(y)|\,/\,|S(x)\cup S(y)| ; a match is exact , written E \mathrm{E} , when J ⁡ ( x , y ) ≥ θ J(x,y)\geq\theta with θ = 0.9 \theta=0.9 , and relaxed , written R \mathrm{R} , when θ ′ ≤ J ⁡ ( x , y ) < θ \theta^{\prime}\leq J(x,y)<\theta with θ ′ = 0.5 \theta^{\prime}=0.5 . State-conditionality is how much the usefulness of an item depends on the current state matching its source state. Once the context route has run with exact-only retrieval C c E {\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}^{\mathrm{E}}} and relaxed-only retrieval C c R {\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}^{\mathrm{R}}} , the online quantity κ ⁡ ( c ) ≜ U ⁡ ( C c E ) − U ⁡ ( C c R ) U ⁡ ( C c E ) − U 0 , ⊳ share of the context gain that needs an exact state match \kappa(c)\;\triangleq\;\frac{\hbox{\pagecolor{AccentC!40}$\displaystyle U({\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}^{\mathrm{E}}})$}\;-\;\hbox{\pagecolor{AccentC!40}$\displaystyle U({\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}^{\mathrm{R}}})$}}{\hbox{\pagecolor{AccentC!40}$\displaystyle U({\color[rgb]{0.5371,0.4039,0.26}C_{c}^{\mathrm{E}}})$}\;-\;U_{0}},\qquad{\color[rgb]{0.35,0.35,0.35}\text{\scriptsize$\triangleright$\,share of the context gain that needs an exact state match}} (4) confirms the proxy, where U 0 = U ⁡ ( π ) U_{0}=U(\pi) is the success of the agent without experience. Both r r and κ 0 \kappa_{0} come from the pool alone, so a practitioner has them before any training decision. Two destinations. The context route keeps D c D_{c} in a library indexed by application and key. The context gain rises with the information gap from +0.2 points in the lowest sixth of the cells to +11.3 in the highest (Spearman 0.65); the producer’s ability tracks it at 0.20 on its own and at 0.05 once the information gap is held fixed, and with the consumer’s headroom on the family held fixed the information gap keeps 0.65. A note pays when it says something the consumer does not know, whoever wrote it. Policy disagreement takes the weights gain away. The weights gain falls with the policy gap from +4.0 points in the lowest sixth to − - 5.7 in the highest ( − - 0.52; − - 0.52 given the information gap) and rises with the information gap (0.49): fine-tuning buys the same information as the notes and pays for it on every state where the producer’s action is one the consumer would not take. 6.2 Producer Shifts Along the ladder. A larger producer widens the information gap, a foreign one opens a policy gap, and each route follows its own. For the Qwen3-VL-8B consumer, the 4B, 8B and 32B producers of its family have information gaps of 0.04, 0.06 and 0.08 and the same policy gap (0.16); their notes gain more in that order, and in the weights only the consumer’s own samples gain (Figure 5 a), the practice term of Equation 6 . A foreign producer is a policy gap, not an information gap. The GUI-Owl-8B pool has the information gap of a same-family producer (0.07) and a policy gap of 0.46: its notes help as much as the consumer’s own, and its samples hurt (Figure 5 b). Retraining that producer on the consumer’s successes closes the policy gap (0.17), leaves the information gap (0.07), and brings its samples to what a same-family producer’s give. 6.3 Consumer Shifts Consumer upgrade. After an upgrade the notes keep their value and the weights start over, because what the weights bought was practice. When the consumer moves from the 8B to the 32B model of the same family, the notes of the 8B producer still give the 32B consumer +3.2 points and the same samples in its weights − - 1.4. Practice needs no producer. On all five consumers, fine-tuning on the consumer’s own successes alone, from families it already solves, matches its full procedures within 1.1 points (Figure 9 d). A note library therefore carries over a change of consumer, and the weights route is rebuilt from the new consumer’s own trajectories. 7 Conclusion We presented component routing, which sends each component of a GUI agent’s own experience to the context or to the weights by two properties measured on the pool before any training, recurrence and state-conditionality. On the same items and held-out tasks across three backbone families and two environments, one pool has two destinations: locators and lessons win in the weights, procedures and state facts in the context. A rule in the two properties recovers the destination of every component on a held-out family and of both halves of a component split at its boundary, and routing by it beats every whole-trajectory baseline and, on average, the better single destination of each backbone. Note readout falls once the same component is in the weights, most for the components that recur most; context gains grow with the information gap and weights gains shrink with the policy gap, so where experience belongs also depends on who produced it and who consumes it.
